chapter: Chapter VI: Of Offences Affecting Life
verbatim_text: Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
plain_summary: Defines the penalty for murder. Any intentional act causing death without legal excuse carries life imprisonment or the death penalty along with a fine. Also introduces specific severe penalties for mob lynching based on caste, religion, or community.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Substituted IPC Section 302; added sub-section (2) addressing murder committed by a group of five or more on protected grounds (mob lynching).

chapter: Chapter VI: Of Offences Affecting Life and Body
verbatim_text: Whoever does any act with the intention of thereby causing hurt to any person, or with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause hurt to any person, and does thereby cause hurt to any person, is said 'voluntarily to cause hurt'. Whoever, except in the case provided for by sub-section (1) of section 122, voluntarily causes hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.
plain_summary: Covers physical assault causing bodily pain, disease, or infirmity. Carries imprisonment up to one year, a fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Corresponds to IPC Section 323; fine amount increased from ₹1,000 to ₹10,000.

chapter: Chapter XVII: Of Offences Against Property
verbatim_text: Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, or dishonestly uses or disposes of that property in violation of any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, commits criminal breach of trust. Whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.
plain_summary: Applies when someone entrusted with your money, vehicle, deposit, or goods dishonestly converts or misuses it (e.g., landlord refusing to return an undisputed security deposit, or an employee embezzling firm funds). Carries imprisonment up to five years, fine, or both.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Consolidates IPC Section 405 definition and Section 406 penalty; enhanced maximum prison term from 3 years to 5 years.

chapter: Chapter XVII: Of Offences Against Property
section_heading: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property
verbatim_text: Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, commits cheating. Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
plain_summary: Defines criminal cheating and fraudulent inducement. Applicable to financial scams, fake online sellers, and fraudulent investment promises. Punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Directly replaces IPC Section 420 (Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property).

chapter: Chapter XIX: Of Criminal Intimidation, Insult and Annoyance
verbatim_text: Whoever threatens another with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of any one in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, commits criminal intimidation. Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
plain_summary: Protects against threats to cause bodily harm, destroy property, or ruin reputation (blackmail, extortion threats). Carries up to two years imprisonment or fine; enhanced to seven years if threat is to cause death or grievous hurt.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Corresponds directly to IPC Section 503 and 506.

chapter: Chapter XX: Miscellaneous
verbatim_text: The Indian Penal Code is hereby repealed. Notwithstanding such repeal, any act done or any investigation, inquiry or proceedings commenced or pending under the repealed Code shall be continued and disposed of in accordance with the provisions of the repealed Code as if this Sanhita had not come into force. The repeal shall not affect the previous operation of the repealed Code or any penalty, forfeiture or punishment incurred in respect of any offence committed against that Code.
plain_summary: Crucial statutory savings clause. Establishes that offences committed prior to July 1, 2024, as well as ongoing investigations and trials, continue to be governed and prosecuted under the Indian Penal Code (IPC 1860).

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Governs the transitional statutory boundary between old and new criminal law.

chapter: Chapter XIII: Information to the Police and Their Powers to Investigate
section_heading: Information in cognizable cases (First Information Report - FIR)
verbatim_text: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant. Every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the State Government may prescribe. Provided that information may be given electronically (e-FIR) to the police officer and shall be taken on record on being signed within three days by the person giving it.
plain_summary: Governs the mandatory registration of an FIR for serious (cognizable) offences. Explicitly codifies the statutory right to submit an e-FIR electronically, provided it is signed within three days by the informant.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Replaces CrPC Section 154; adds statutory recognition for electronic communication / e-FIR with a 3-day signature window.

chapter: Chapter XXXVIII: Miscellaneous
verbatim_text: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is hereby repealed. Notwithstanding such repeal, if, immediately before the date on which this Sanhita comes into force, there is any appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending, then, such appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation shall be disposed of, continued, held or made, as the case may be, in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, as in force immediately before such commencement, as if this Sanhita had not come into force.
plain_summary: Procedural savings clause. Guarantees that pending police investigations, criminal trials, applications, and appeals initiated prior to July 1, 2024 proceed under the old CrPC 1973 rules.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Governs procedural continuity between CrPC and BNSS.

chapter: Chapter I: Preliminary
verbatim_text: 'Deficiency' means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service and includes any act of negligence or omission or commission by such person which causes loss or injury to the consumer, and deliberate withholding of relevant information by such person to the consumer.
plain_summary: Defines what legally constitutes 'deficiency in service'. Includes delayed deliveries, substandard repairs, unexplained bank deductions, wrongful flight cancellations, and withholding essential terms from the customer.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Expanded definition to explicitly include deliberate withholding of relevant information and e-commerce service omissions.

legal_attributes.triable_by: District / State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission

chapter: Chapter IV: Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
section_heading: Manner in which complaint shall be made
verbatim_text: A complaint, in relation to any goods sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or any service provided or agreed to be provided, may be filed with a District Commission by the consumer, or any recognized consumer association, or the Central Authority. A complaint may also be filed electronically in such manner as may be prescribed (e-Daakhil), and fees in respect of such complaint shall be paid electronically. The District Commission shall ordinarily decide on admissibility within twenty-one days.
plain_summary: Details how a citizen can lodge a formal consumer complaint with the District Commission, including the statutory right to file online via e-Daakhil from anywhere in India without hiring an advocate. The commission must decide admissibility within 21 days.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Introduced electronic filing (e-Daakhil) and jurisdiction based on where the consumer resides rather than where the seller is located.

chapter: Chapter XI: Offences
verbatim_text: Whoever, fraudulently or dishonestly make use of the electronic signature, password or any other unique identification feature of any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend with rupees one lakh.
plain_summary: Protects against unauthorized use of your digital identity, including stolen passwords, OTPs, forged electronic signatures, Aadhaar biometric misuse, and hacked social media accounts. Punishable by up to 3 years imprisonment and ₹1,00,000 fine.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Specialized penal statute for digital identity hijacking.

legal_attributes.triable_by: Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate First Class

chapter: Chapter XI: Offences
section_heading: Punishment for cheating by personation by using computer resource
verbatim_text: Whoever, by means of any communication device or computer resource cheats by personation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to one lakh rupees.
plain_summary: Direct legal remedy for cyber phishing, fake bank executive phone calls, impersonation on WhatsApp/Telegram, and online scam operations. Carries up to 3 years in prison and a fine up to ₹1,00,000.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Primary section cited alongside BNS Section 318 in cyber financial fraud FIRs.

legal_attributes.triable_by: Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate First Class

act_title: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
chapter: Chapter II: Domestic Violence
verbatim_text: For the purposes of this Act, any act, omission or commission or conduct of the respondent shall constitute domestic violence if it harms or injures or endangers the health, safety, life, limb or well-being, whether mental or physical, of the aggrieved person or tends to do so and includes causing physical abuse, sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse and economic abuse; or harasses, harms, injures or endangers the aggrieved person with a view to coerce her or any other person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any dowry or other property.
plain_summary: Provides a comprehensive civil-remedy definition of domestic abuse. Covers physical violence, sexual abuse, emotional/verbal insults (constant humiliation, denying children), and economic abuse (depriving of financial resources, denying access to household items or maintenance).

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Civil remedy mechanism allowing immediate emergency protection and residence orders without requiring criminal prosecution.

legal_attributes.triable_by: Judicial Magistrate of the first class / Metropolitan Magistrate

act_title: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
chapter: Chapter IV: Procedure for Obtaining Orders of Reliefs
verbatim_text: An aggrieved person or a Protection Officer or any other person on behalf of the aggrieved person may present an application to the Magistrate seeking one or more reliefs under this Act. The Magistrate shall fix the first date of hearing, which shall not ordinarily be beyond three days from the date of receipt of the application by the court. The Magistrate shall endeavour to dispose of every application within a period of sixty days from the date of its first hearing.
plain_summary: Allows an aggrieved woman or a Protection Officer to file an application before a Magistrate for emergency protection, maintenance, or residence orders. The court must hold the first hearing within 3 days and aim to dispose of the matter within 60 days.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Fast-track relief window with statutory 3-day first hearing timeline.

legal_attributes.triable_by: Judicial Magistrate of the first class

chapter: Chapter VI: Entitlement to Legal Services
verbatim_text: Every person who has to file or defend a case shall be entitled to legal services under this Act if that person, is a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe; a victim of trafficking in human beings or begar; a woman or a child; a person with disability; a person under circumstances of underserved want such as being a victim of a mass disaster, ethnic violence, caste atrocity, flood, drought, earthquake or industrial disaster; an industrial workman; in custody; or in receipt of annual income less than the amount specified by the State Government if the case is before a court other than the Supreme Court.
plain_summary: Codifies who has a statutory right to free government legal representation and court fee waivers across India. Women, children, SC/ST citizens, disabled persons, and low-income citizens qualify automatically. Note: Final advocate assignment is granted upon formal DLSA review.

transition_mapping.historical_section: Primary statutory gateway for legal aid
transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Establishes National, State, District, and Taluka legal services entitlement.

chapter: Chapter XVII: Of Penalties in Case of Dishonour of Certain Cheques
section_heading: Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account
verbatim_text: Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both. Provided that statutory notice must be sent within 30 days of receiving return memo, and complaint filed within one month thereafter.
plain_summary: Defines the penal procedure for bounced cheques. Mandates strict procedural timelines: a formal statutory notice must be served on the drawer within 30 days of dishonour memo; the drawer is given 15 days to pay; if unpaid, a criminal complaint must be filed within one month. Punishable by up to 2 years imprisonment, a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both.

transition_mapping.historical_section: Amended by Act 55 of 2002 and Act 20 of 2018
transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Enhanced penalty to 2 years and introduced interim compensation provisions under Section 143A.

legal_attributes.triable_by: Judicial Magistrate of the first class / Metropolitan Magistrate

chapter: Chapter V: Of Leases of Immovable Property
section_heading: Rights and liabilities of lessor and lessee
verbatim_text: In the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary, the lessor and the lessee of immovable property, as against one another, respectively, possess the rights and are subject to the liabilities mentioned in the rules following: The lessor is bound to disclose to the lessee any material defect in the property; the lessor is bound on the lessee's request to put him in possession of the property; and upon termination of the lease, the lessee is bound to put the lessor into possession, and the lessor is bound to account for and refund any deposit or advance held in trust.
plain_summary: Defines core tenancy rights. Establishes that landlords cannot arbitrarily dispossess tenants without following the legal process of law, and are statutorily bound to refund security deposits upon lawful determination of lease, subject to agreed terms.

transition_mapping.historical_section: Complemented by State Rent Control Acts & Model Tenancy Act 2021
transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Central common-law standard for leases.

chapter: Chapter II: Right to Information and Obligations of Public Authorities
verbatim_text: A person, who desires to obtain any information under this Act, shall make a request in writing or through electronic means in English or Hindi or in the official language of the area in which the application is being made, accompanying such fee as may be prescribed, to the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer. An applicant making request for information shall not be required to give any reason for requesting the information or any other personal details except those that may be necessary for contacting him.
plain_summary: Empowers any Indian citizen to file an RTI request with any public authority in English, Hindi, or regional languages. Explicitly provides that the citizen is NOT required to give any justification or reason for seeking information.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Created universal public transparency mechanism with strict 30-day timeline.

chapter: V - Of Documentary Evidence
verbatim_text: Nothing in this Adhiniyam shall apply to deny the admissibility of an electronic record in evidence on the ground that it is an electronic record, and such record shall have the same legal effect, validity and enforceability as other document, subject to the provisions of section 63.
plain_summary: Electronic records (emails, WhatsApp messages, SMS, digital invoices, and CCTV footage) are recognized as primary documentary evidence in Indian courts, possessing the same legal force as physical documents subject to Section 63 certificate verification.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Replaces Section 65B certificate framework; provides unified statutory recognition for digital records and modern cloud/device storage.

chapter: V - Of Documentary Evidence
section_heading: Special provisions as to evidence relating to electronic record
verbatim_text: Any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on a paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media produced by a computer shall be deemed to be also a document... and shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, if the conditions specified in this section are satisfied.
plain_summary: Mandates an Electronic Evidence Certificate signed by the person in lawful control of the device or an expert, verifying device integrity and contemporaneous storage conditions for printouts and digital evidence to be admitted without original device production.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Modernizes certificate procedure, incorporating Schedule-based statutory forms and expert/custodian signatures.

chapter: XXXV - Provisions as to Bail and Bonds
section_heading: Maximum period for which an undertrial prisoner can be detained
verbatim_text: Where a person has, during the period of investigation, inquiry or trial under this Sanhita of an offence under any law... undergone detention for a period extending up to one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for that offence under that law, he shall be released by the Court on bail: Provided that where such person is a first-time offender... he shall be released on bail if he has undergone detention for a period extending up to one-third of the maximum period of imprisonment.
plain_summary: Mandatory statutory bail for undertrials: first-time offenders who have spent one-third of the maximum sentence in detention must be released on personal bond; all other undertrials must be released upon completing one-half of maximum term.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Liberalized undertrial relief: introduced novel 1/3rd detention threshold for first-time offenders to decongest prisons.

chapter: XVII - Of Offences Against Property
verbatim_text: Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that persons consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft. Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
plain_summary: Dishonestly moving or taking any movable property out of a persons possession without their consent constitutes theft, punishable with up to 3 years imprisonment, fine, or community service for petty cases under 5,000 rupees upon return.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Subsumes definitions and punishment; adds community service provision for petty theft.

chapter: V - Of Offences Against Women and Children
section_heading: Assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty
verbatim_text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any woman, intending to outrage or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby outrage her modesty, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine.
plain_summary: Physical assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage modesty carries a mandatory minimum of 1 year up to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fine. Strictly non-bailable and cognizable.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Re-enacted with identical elements and minimum sentence guarantees under unified Chapter V.

chapter: IV - Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
verbatim_text: Subject to the other provisions of this Act, the District Commission shall have jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed fifty lakh rupees. A complaint may be filed in District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the complainant resides or personally works for gain.
plain_summary: District Consumer Commission has pecuniary jurisdiction up to ₹50 lakh consideration value (amended from ₹1 crore by 2021 rules). Crucially permits consumers to file complaints where they currently reside or work, eliminating requirement to travel to the sellers registered office.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Enhanced pecuniary limit and introduced consumer-residence filing jurisdiction plus online e-Daakhil filing.

chapter: V - Of Leases of Immovable Property
section_heading: Duration of certain leases in absence of written contract or local usage
verbatim_text: In the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by six months notice; and a lease of immovable property for any other purpose shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by fifteen days notice.
plain_summary: Tenancy termination notice requirement: in residential and commercial leases without contrary written agreement, either landlord or tenant must give at least 15 days written notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy before seeking possession.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Amended in 2002 to protect notice validity from technical defects; 15-day period commences from receipt.

chapter: II - Right to Information and Obligations of Public Authorities
verbatim_text: The Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer... shall, as expeditiously as possible, and in any case within thirty days of the receipt of the request, either provide the information on payment of such fee as may be prescribed or reject the request: Provided that where the information sought for concerns the life or liberty of a person, the same shall be provided within forty-eight hours of the receipt of the request.
plain_summary: Statutory time limits for government information: mandatory 30 days for general RTI requests, and mandatory 48 hours where the information concerns personal life or liberty. Failure to respond within timeline is deemed refusal and triggers penalty under Section 20.

transition_mapping.nature_of_change: Replaced toothless 2002 law with binding timeframes, nominal fees, and personal officer penalties.
